intent: I manage a business, institutional or association property in Duval, St. Johns, Nassau or Clay County and want turf for a courtyard, dog run or play area. Does Florida's synthetic turf law protect or limit that, do I need a stormwater permit, does turf count toward required landscaping, and do the county landscape codes reach an existing site?
distinctValue: The national commercial page says only 'check with the responsible reviewer', and the Denver and Grand Strand pages deal with Colorado's nonfunctional-turf law and Horry County's stormwater fee. This page tells a northeast Florida buyer that DEP says Rule 62-308.100 (effective 19 May 2026) does not apply to commercial properties and runs no permit, inspection or enforcement program, and that the s. 125.572 limits (2026 Florida Statutes, as amended by ch. 2026-164 to exclude a CDD enforcing deed restrictions) are tied to single-family residential standards; that Rule 62-330.020 sets ERP thresholds (more than 4,000 sq ft vehicular and 9,000 sq ft total impervious and semi-impervious area, part of a larger common plan, modification of a permitted project) with carve-outs, and the SJRWMD handbook's impervious and semi-impervious definitions never name turf, with a 10 percent or 0.5 acre modification factor; that Clay County Sec. 18.5-53 and Nassau County Sec. 37.05 bar synthetic material from substituting for required plants, while St. Johns LDC 6.06.02.A.5 bars only 'artificial plants' and its impervious definition names wet retention areas but not turf; when Nassau 37.05 and Jacksonville 656.1209 reach an existing site (redevelopment thresholds of 7,500/750/2,000 sq ft and 10 percent; 60 percent renovation or expansion for commercial), and that St. Johns Section 13.16 governs changes to approved construction plans; and that Atlantic Beach's undated guidelines apply to all installations with 100 in/hr permeability, a 4-inch aggregate base, retention-area conditions, required documents and a base inspection.

sources.label: Rule 62-308.100, F.A.C.: adopted rule text
supports: (b) Pursuant to s. 125.572, F.S., this rule establishes minimum standards for the installation of synthetic turf on single-family residential properties of 1 acre or less in size. Pursuant to s. 125.572(3), F.S., local governments may not regulate synthetic turf in a manner inconsistent with these minimum standards. This rule does not establish nor require any new department-issued permit or authorization for the installation of synthetic turf,

(c) Infill material, if used, shall only be clean silica sand, rock, shell, or other natural material, except that coated silica sand may be used provided that any coating used is non-toxic and meets the requirements described in paragraphs (2)(a) and (2)(b). sources.label: Florida DEP: Synthetic Turf FAQ
supports: Does this rule apply to condominiums, duplexes, parks, athletic fields or commercial properties? No. This rule only applies to single-family residential properties that are 1 acre or less in size.

Instead, this rule establishes minimum standards that local governments must use when adopting or enforcing any ordinance, resolution, order, rule or policy relating to the installation of synthetic turf on single-family residential properties 1 acre or less in size.
Does DEP inspect or enforce synthetic turf installations? No. DEP is not implementing a permitting, inspection or enforcement program under this rule.
Does this rule regulate Homeowners' Associations (HOAs) or private deed restrictions? No. This rule does not address HOA requirements, deed restrictions or other private property agreements.

sources.label: The 2026 Florida Statutes, s. 125.572 (Regulation of synthetic turf)
supports: (3)(a) Upon the Department of Environmental Protection adopting rules pursuant to subsection (4), a local government may not: 1. Adopt or enforce any ordinance, resolution, order, rule, or policy that prohibits, or is enforced to prohibit, a property owner from installing synthetic turf that complies with Department of Environmental Protection standards adopted pursuant to this section which apply to single-family residential property.

2. Adopt or enforce any ordinance, resolution, order, rule, or policy that regulates synthetic turf which is inconsistent with the Department of Environmental Protection standards adopted pursuant to this section which apply to single-family residential property.
(b) This subsection does not apply to the adoption or enforcement of any resolution, order, rule, or policy by a community development district to enforce deed restrictions.

sources.label: Rule 62-330.020, F.A.C.: regulated activities (current rule text)
supports: (1) A permit under this chapter is not required for activities that qualify for: (a) Operation and routine custodial maintenance of projects legally in existence under Chapter 403 or Part IV of Chapter 373, F.S., provided the terms and conditions of the permit, exemption, or other authorization for such projects continue to be met, and provided the activity is conducted in a manner that does not cause violations of state water quality standards. However, this exemption shall not apply to any project that is altered, modified, expanded, abandoned, or removed;

(b) An exemption listed in Rule 62-330.051 or 62-330.0511, F.A.C., or in section 1.3 (District-specific exemptions) of the applicable Volume II; (c) The “grandfathering” provisions of Section 373.4131(4), 373.414(11), (12)(a), (13), (14), (15), or (16), F.S.; or (d) The “10/2” general permit for upland stormwater systems authorized in Section 403.814(12), F.S.

(2) Unless the activity qualifies under subsection (1), above, a permit is required prior to the construction, alteration, operation, maintenance, removal, or abandonment of any project that, by itself or in combination with an activity conducted after October 1, 2013, cumulatively results in any of the following:

(a) Any project in, on, or over wetlands or other surface waters; (b) A total of more than 4,000 square feet of impervious and semi-impervious surface areas subject to vehicular traffic; (c) A total of more than 9,000 square feet of impervious and semi-impervious surface area; (d) A total project area of more than five acres;
(g) Any project that is part of a larger common plan of development or sale;
(j) Any modification or alteration of a project previously permitted under Part IV of Chapter 373, F.S.
History–New 10-1-13, Amended 6-1-18.

sources.label: Nassau County Land Development Code, Sec. 37.05 (Landscaping), Municode (codified through Ord. No. 2026-032)
supports: A. Applicability. 1. The standards established in this section are to be considered the minimum requirements for the design, plant selection, installation and maintenance of landscape elements and site improvements and shall apply to all new development.

2. Developments constructed under previously effective landscaping requirements are not required to comply with this section. However, the requirements of this section shall also apply to the redevelopment, reconfiguration, expansion or change of use of a previously developed site, unless such change falls below the following threshold:

a. The existing developed impervious area is seven thousand five hundred (7,500) square feet or less, and the proposed expansion of impervious surface is seven hundred fifty (750) square feet or less. b. The existing developed impervious area is greater than seven thousand five hundred (7,500) square feet, and the proposed expansion of impervious surface is less than two thousand (2,000) square feet, and also less than ten percent (10%) of the existing impervious area on the parcel or lot.
Synthetic or artificial trees, shrubs, groundcovers or vines are not acceptable substitutes.
Codified through Ordinance No. 2026-032, enacted April 27, 2026. (Supp. No. 17)

sources.label: City of Atlantic Beach: Artificial Turf Installation Guidelines (undated; PDF metadata shows it was created 14 May 2026)
supports: Artificial turf is permitted within the City of Atlantic Beach when installed in a manner that maintains proper drainage, protects trees, and preserves public infrastructure. The following standards apply to all artificial turf installations.
Turf systems must provide a minimum permeability rate of 100 inches per hour.
Artificial turf must be installed over a minimum 4-inch deep permeable, free-draining aggregate base.
Artificial turf may be installed within privately owned stormwater retention, or drainage areas provided the installation does not reduce the designed storage capacity or function of the system.
Artificial turf may not obstruct drainage structures, overflow paths, or maintenance access.
The City may require engineering documentation demonstrating that stormwater capacity and drainage performance are maintained.
Manufacturer product specifications; Permeability testing documentation; Installation details or cross-section drawings; Site plan showing locations relative to trees and property lines
The aggregate subbase must be inspected and approved before turf installation.
